newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Ex-communists rebuffed in Bulgaria, Romania.
newsitem.headline: Ex-communists rebuffed in Bulgaria, Romania.

text.p: Voters dealt a sharp rebuff to ex-communists in an election in Bulgaria and threatened another in the neighbouring Balkan state of Romania.
But in Yugoslavia, in the first poll since the end of a four-year Balkan war, the ruling leftist coalition of Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic was cruising to election victory.
In Bulgaria, the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) won a huge boost when its candidate, lawyer Petar Stoyanov, pulled off a convincing win in Sunday's presidential election.
With a third of polling station returns counted, official results showed Stoyanov, 44, leading with more than 61 percent of the vote to Socialist Culture Minister Ivan Marazov's 39 percent.

Although the president of the former Warsaw Pact country has few powers and the Socialists will remain in government, Prime Minister Zhan Videnov said the party had to take note of the electorate's strong message of disapproval.
"We have important, radical and maybe painful decisions to take in the interests of the country," Videnov told reporters.
He said a party congress could be held as early as January and did not rule out cabinet changes.

Across the border in Romania -- like Bulgaria another former member of the Soviet camp -- voters appeared to have overturned seven years of ex-communist rule, rejecting President Ion Iliescu's ruling party in parliamentary elections.
Exit polls showed the Democratic Convention (CDR), a grouping of 15 parties under professor Emil Constantinescu, in front with 32 to 35 percent of the vote.
Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), which along with its predecessor has run Romania since the 1989 fall of communism, was well back with between 22 and 25 percent.
If the exit polls are confirmed by official results, due to trickle in from late on Monday, the election will mark a stunning shift in Romanian politics.
But Iliescu's personal fate will be decided in a presidential race.
Here, the polls produced a split verdict, but it was clear Iliescu and Constantinescu would contest a run-off in two weeks' time.

The pattern was not repeated however in Yugoslavia where Milosevic was leading his leftist coalition to victory, winning popular endorsement for his new peace-making policies despite a troubled economy.

"It is not a question whether we are going to win. It is rather the question of how resounding our victory will be," Slobodan Cerovic, a leading member of the influential coalition partner Yugoslav United Left (JUL), told Reuters.
JUL headed by Milosevic's wife Mirjana Markovic forms the leftist coalition with New Democracy and Milosevic's Socialist Party SPS.

According to initial results from the federal and municipal elections, announced by SPS spokesman Ivica Dacic, the left was winning in nearly all the major towns in Serbia proper and its Vojvodina and Kosovo provinces.

A low voter turnout of 61 percent, reported by the federal election commission, was bad news for the opposition as Milosevic's coalition parties rely on loyal followers -- many of them pensioners -- with disciplined voting habits.
Opposition leaders blamed the state-run media, ethnic Albanians, lack of interest by the West and lethargy by voters for their poor performance.
The low turnout testified to the widespread apathy among the population. Almost a third now lives in poverty, according to a Red Cross survey.
A year of peace and the end of a U.N. trade embargo has failed to bring economic relief to a country which once enjoyed the highest standard of living in Eastern Europe.
The elections were the first major test for Milosevic's new peace-making policies, highlighted as the leading achievement by the ruling coalition to cover up a bad economic situation.
